tagline.text: A memorial obelisk standing where the Death March finally ended

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–2,000 per person (day trip from Manila)

image.credit: jopetsy from Metro Manila, Philippines / CC BY 2.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A national memorial park built on the site of Camp O'Donnell, where tens of thousands of Filipino and American prisoners died at the end of the Bataan Death March. An obelisk about 73m tall, a memorial wall inscribed with over 30,000 names, and a forest with one tree planted for every victim quietly bear witness to that time.

Capas National Shrine is a World War II memorial park in Aranguren village, Capas, Tarlac. This is the site of Camp O'Donnell, where Japanese forces imprisoned Filipino and American allied POWs starting in

, and the final destination of the Bataan Death March. On the roughly 54-hectare grounds stand an obelisk, a memorial wall, and national monuments, with most of the area a forest of trees planted in memory of the victims.
After Allied forces on the Bataan peninsula surrendered on
April 9, 1942
, tens of thousands of prisoners were forced to walk about
100km

under the blazing sun from Mariveles to San Fernando, Pampanga. At San Fernando station they were packed into freight cars too cramped to breathe properly, then unloaded at Capas station and marched on foot again to the camp. Many collapsed during the march itself, and records show that over the following months, more than 20,000 Filipinos and about 1,500 Americans died at the camp from starvation, malaria, and dysentery.
The shrine was declared a national shrine in
, and the park's signature obelisk was unveiled on
April 9, 2003
. It's managed by the Philippine Veterans Affairs Office (PVAO), and every
April 9
, Araw ng Kagitingan (Day of Valor), veterans, families of the fallen, and government officials gather here for a memorial ceremony.

There's no dramatic sightseeing here, but standing before the endless rows of trees and the black memorial wall, you quietly feel the weight of the war. Recommended for travelers interested in World War II history, and those who want to teach history to their families. Since it's in Capas, the starting point for Mount Pinatubo tours, it pairs well with Pinatubo or Monasterio de Tarlac.
The white obelisk rising about
at the center of the park symbolizes peace. A bell hangs at its base, and looking up from inside, the tower's lines stretching toward the sky make a striking sight.

The black marble wall curving around the obelisk is inscribed with the names of over 30,000 people who died at the camp and during the march. Walk slowly along the wall, where Filipino and American names appear side by side.
The park holds about 31,000 trees, one planted for each victim. Walking the shaded paths between the rows of trees, the deaths feel real as individual lives, not just a number.

blocks.title: The prisoner transport freight car display

children.text: An old railway freight car, matching the type prisoners were packed into like cargo from San Fernando to Capas, is on display. Reading that nearly a hundred people were crammed into one small car leaves a somber impression.

Memorial spaces for different nations are scattered around the park, including the Omnia Pro Patria Cross honoring American victims and a monument to Filipino soldiers. Reading the inscriptions and dedications as you walk around,
1–2 hours
passes quickly.

The long, straight walkway from the flagpole to the obelisk is popular with locals for morning and evening walks and cycling. Walking it in the cool morning gives you a real sense of the park's scale.

Visiting the old San Fernando train station and Death March markers around Capas together links the prisoners' route into a single story. Pairing it with the Shrine of Valor at Mount Samat in Bataan makes for an even deeper history trip.

Some Mount Pinatubo day tours offer an option to stop at Capas National Shrine on the way back. Check whether it's included when you book.
The Tarlac plain has a dry season,
November–April
December–February
has relatively cool mornings, good for walking the large park, while
March–May
sees midday temperatures climb to around
, making the shadeless walkway and obelisk plaza very hot. Visit around
during this period.
In the wet season,
June–October

, showers and typhoons are frequent, but the site remains open. During heavy rain, though, the lawns get muddy and walking is uncomfortable. For a deeper sense of the site's historical weight, consider visiting around
April 9

, Day of Valor. That day draws crowds for the memorial ceremony, and some areas may have restricted access. For a quiet visit, a weekday morning with no event is best, and sunset behind the obelisk is a calm, beautiful sight too.

With almost no lodging around the shrine, most visitors come for the day. If you're staying over, use a business hotel in Tarlac City (about
per night), about
30–40 minutes
away by car, or a hotel or resort in Clark/Angeles (about
), about
40 minutes–1 hour
away. New lodging is also growing around New Clark City. If you're combining this with a Pinatubo tour, staying in Capas or Clark, close to the tour's starting point, is convenient.

There's no restaurant inside the shrine, just a small shop near the entrance selling drinks and snacks. Eat at a carinderia (local eatery) in downtown Capas or in Tarlac City. Tarlac blends Pampanga, Ilocos, and Pangasinan influences, so you can try Kapampangan braised dishes alongside Ilocano vegetable dishes in the same area. If food is a priority, heading down to Clark/Angeles for original sisig and Kapampangan cuisine is also a good option.
The park is large with many shadeless stretches. Be sure to bring a hat, a parasol, and water.
Hours are generally
8 AM–5 PM
, but can change for events or maintenance, so check before you visit.
If you want to find a family member's or acquaintance's name on the memorial wall, ask the caretaker at the entrance for help.
Reading up on the Death March and Camp O'Donnell's history beforehand makes the park's meaning land much more powerfully.
If you arrive by public transport, arrange your return tricycle in advance. Vehicles don't pass by the shrine's entrance often.
If combining this with a Pinatubo tour on the same day, a morning trek followed by an afternoon visit here works well.

If you're bringing children, explain the story of the war and the prisoners in an age-appropriate way beforehand. Telling them that each tree represents one person is something kids grasp easily and remember for a long time.
Drone photography may require permission from the management office. Ask in advance.

If you plan to combine it with a Pinatubo tour on the Capas side, foreign visitors need permission to visit from the Philippine Air Force, and must submit a passport copy through the tour operator about
35 days
before the visit. An itinerary that sees only the shrine without permission has no such restriction.
Usually in
late February to early March

, the Bataan Freedom March, held by the Philippine Veterans Bank with the Philippine Veterans Affairs Office (PVAO) and the Department of National Defense, walks the old Death March route from Mariveles over more than two days and ends with a commemoration at this shrine (in
it arrived on
March 1
). It can be crowded with events around then, so if you want to take part or watch, check the organizers' notices.
This is a memorial space where tens of thousands died. Don't climb on or lean against the memorial wall or monuments for photos — view the site quietly.
There's a risk of heatstroke at midday in
March–May
. Avoid walking around at midday and drink plenty of water.
Official events like Day of Valor may involve security checks and access restrictions. Check the latest notices.
There are military facilities in the surrounding area. Don't enter posted restricted zones, and refrain from photographing military installations.
Admission fees and hours can change. Follow on-site guidance.
